summary: Proposes the Internet Routing Overlay Network, an overlay to support growth without changing end systems or the existing routing system. It also addresses mobility and multihoming. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A new layer of roads laid over the old ones to ease traffic jams, without rebuilding the old roads.

does iron require changes to existing routers
subtitle: An overlay network for scalable routing without changing the Internet.

tldr.problem: The Internet's routing system is strained by growth in the number of routes, especially from multihoming and provider-independent addressing. Fixing this requires new routing methodologies.
tldr.mechanism: IRON creates a virtual overlay network on top of the existing Internet. Virtual Prefix Companies (VPCs) own prefixes, operate routers (Servers, Relays, Clients), and tunnel traffic through the overlay using encapsulation, reducing the number of routes in the core.
tldr.outcome: Supports sustainable growth and addresses mobility, multihoming, and traffic engineering without requiring changes to end systems or the existing routing system. It is experimental and requires deployment of new infrastructure.

today: RFC 6179 is an Experimental specification published by the IRTF Routing Research Group. It has not been widely deployed and remains a research proposal for addressing Internet routing scaling challenges.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet routing system has grown to handle millions of routes, but this growth is unsustainable. The problem is driven by multihoming (customers using multiple internet providers) and the use of provider-independent addresses, both of which force more and more specific routing prefixes into the core Internet. IPv4 address space depletion makes this worse.

IRON (the Internet Routing Overlay Network) proposes a solution that adds a new layer on top of the existing Internet. Rather than changing how hosts or most routers work, IRON introduces specialized routers and servers operated by companies that manage virtual prefixes. These entities tunnel traffic through the existing Internet using encapsulation, dramatically reducing the number of routes core routers must store.
sections.eli5: The Internet's routing tables are getting too big. IRON adds a new layer on top that groups traffic together, so the core routers don't have to know about every tiny route.

sections.title: Architecture and Key Components
sections.content:
IRON comprises three types of agents: Clients, Servers, and Relays. A Client is typically a customer's router that connects an end-user network (called an EUN) to the IRON. It obtains prefixes (called EPs, or End User Network Prefixes) from a Virtual Prefix Company (VPC) and tunnels traffic to a nearby Server.

A Server is operated by a VPC and acts as a tunnel endpoint. It caches the mapping of which Client owns each prefix, forwards packets from Clients toward their destinations, and can optimize routes by sending redirect messages. Servers are distributed globally so that Clients can reach a nearby one. A Relay is also operated by a VPC and sits at the border between the IRON overlay and the native Internet. Relays advertise the VPC's virtual prefixes into the global BGP routing system and forward traffic between the overlay and the public Internet.

The three components form a hierarchy: Clients connect EUNs to Servers, Servers connect to Relays, and Relays connect to the public Internet. This arrangement allows traffic to be routed and optimized within the overlay without burdening the core Internet routers.
sections.eli5: Clients are customer routers. Servers are distribution hubs run by companies that own prefixes. Relays are border routers that talk to the outside world. Together, they form a shortcut layer on top of the Internet.

sections.title: How Traffic Flows Through IRON
sections.content:
When a host in an IRON EUN sends a packet, the Client router encapsulates it with outer headers and sends it to the Client's selected Server. The outer headers use locator addresses (regular Internet addresses) so the packet can traverse the public Internet, while the inner packet retains the end-user prefix (EP) addresses.

The Server examines the inner destination address. If it is an EP belonging to another IRON EUN, the Server rewrites the outer headers and forwards the packet toward the appropriate Relay. The Relay, upon receiving the packet, looks up the EP and determines which Server serves that endpoint. The Relay sends the packet to that Server and also sends a redirect message back, telling the original Client about the better route. Subsequent packets from that Client can skip the initial Server and Relay and go directly to the destination Server, optimizing the path.

If the inner destination is not an IRON address (a non-IRON host on the public Internet), the Relay simply decapsulates the packet and forwards it unencapsulated into the Internet. Packets flowing in the reverse direction—from non-IRON hosts to IRON EUNs—arrive at a Relay, which encapsulates them and sends them through the overlay to the correct Server and Client.
sections.eli5: A customer's router wraps a packet in an outer envelope so it can travel the Internet. When it reaches the right place, the envelope gets swapped for a better route, or it gets unwrapped and sent to the destination.

sections.title: Mobility, Multihoming, and Renumbering
sections.content:
IRON naturally supports mobility: when a Client changes its network attachment point (e.g., a mobile network), it can update its locator address with its Server. The Server updates its mappings, and existing conversations are redirected without packet loss. Multihoming is also built in—a Client can register multiple locators with its Server and assign metrics to prefer some paths over others.

One key benefit of IRON is stable addressing. Customers obtain their EP prefixes from a VPC, not from their ISP. This means a customer can change ISPs without renumbering their network—the EP prefixes remain the same because they come from the VPC overlay, not the ISP's routing system. This breaks the traditional coupling between network addresses and service providers.
sections.eli5: If a company moves offices, its network addresses stay the same because they come from the overlay, not the Internet provider. When a mobile user moves, the network just tells the server about the new location.

sections.title: Design Principles and Deployment Model
sections.content:
IRON requires no changes to end systems or most existing routers. Only the Client, Server, and Relay agents need to be deployed. These can be added incrementally to the Internet without disruption. Clients may use private addresses behind NATs; the IRON system discovers the actual addresses used by the NAT (IP and UDP port) and uses them as locators.

The system works by having each VPC operate a small set of new infrastructure—Servers and Relays—distributed globally. VPCs coordinate independently; a central registry simply tracks which prefixes belong to which VPC overlay network. This design allows competition between VPCs and keeps the system decentralized.

IRON targets the middle ground between pure routing (which scales poorly) and pure mapping systems (which require global coordination). It borrows ideas from Virtual Aggregation, the RANGER architecture, and the Ivip proposal. The system handles path MTU discovery, multicast proxying, and nested EUNs (where a Client's locator is itself an EP address from another Client).
sections.eli5: No one has to change their computers or existing routers. Only new infrastructure gets added. Small companies or ISPs can operate their own overlay networks.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Future Direction
sections.content:
RFC 6179 is published as an Experimental specification by the IRTF Routing Research Group. It represents research into scalable routing and is not an Internet Standard. The document was considered controversial within the RRG, but there was consensus that it should be published for examination and evaluation. The system has not been widely deployed.

The main open questions involve business considerations (how would VPCs compete and set pricing), operational complexity (managing global Server and Relay deployments), and whether the added indirection would introduce acceptable latency. The RFC notes that these business and operational aspects are out of scope but essential for real-world adoption.
sections.eli5: This is an experimental idea published for researchers to study. It is not an official Internet standard, and no one is using it yet. It might work, but we need to learn more.
